paras: The killing of Tom Weaver was the fatal shooting of Tom Weaver, a Black man, by a posse of citizens at or near Seville, Georgia, on August 22, 1910. Weaver was accused of having fired a shotgun at Mayor Wilson, and the reports differ on whether he was shot down in the town's streets or killed in an exchange of fire at a house a few miles away. A brief wire dispatch carried the story to papers in New York, New Jersey, Connecticut and Wisconsin, while the Americus Times-Recorder printed a fuller report under a headline saying he had been "hanged by posse."

The Times-Recorder described Seville as "a small station on the Seaboard Air Line railway, about twelve miles east of Cordele"; the wire dispatch, datelined Cordele, put it about ten miles away. According to the wire report, Weaver had been fined by the mayor for drunkenness on the preceding Saturday and "threatened at the time to get even." The Times-Recorder's correspondent gave a different sequence, in which Weaver, "on a drunken spree" the night before, had words with Mayor Wilson and resisted arrest, then went to Cordele, bought a shotgun, loaded it with buckshot and returned to Seville.

Weaver was said to have gone to Mayor Wilson's home, called him out and fired at him, missing; the Times-Recorder wrote that the load came "just missing his head." He then fled. In the wire version, he "was caught as he raced through the streets and shot to death by citizens."

The Times-Recorder instead reported that Mayor Wilson and a posse chased him to a small house a few miles from Seville, where Weaver opened fire as they tried to arrest him and was killed in the exchange of shots about midnight Monday. It added that "The members of the posse escaped injury."
No report of an inquest, an arrest or any legal proceeding over the killing appears in the coverage, and none of the papers named anyone who fired the fatal shots.

The story first appeared in the New York Sun on August 23 under the headline "Kill Mayor's Assailant" and the deck "Georgia Citizens Shoot Negro to Death in the Streets." The Iowa County Democrat of Mineral Point, Wisconsin, ran the same dispatch, dated a day later, under "Tom Weaver Pays Penalty for Attempt on Mayor Wilson's Life," presenting the killing as a punishment. Condensed versions in the "Crimes and Casualties" columns of the Monmouth Inquirer of Freehold, New Jersey, and the Connecticut Western News on August 25 made Wilson the mayor "of Cordele."

The Americus Times-Recorder, the only Georgia paper in the coverage, ran its special report on the front page on August 24 headed "Negro Shot at Mayor Is Hanged by Posse," although its own text said Weaver was shot. It called the pursuers "a posse of infuriated citizens" and cast the chase as an effort to arrest a man who fired first. Every account identified Weaver only as "a negro," stated the accusation against him as fact and named none of his pursuers except the mayor. The coverage found consists of these white papers; no Black-press report of the killing was located.

The accounts differ on how and where Weaver died: the wire said he was caught running through the streets of Seville and shot, while the Times-Recorder said he was killed in a gunfight at a house outside town after firing on the posse. The Times-Recorder report came from its own Cordele correspondent and is the more detailed, but neither version names its source or gives Weaver's side.

They also differ on timing: the Sun's dispatch of August 22 placed the attack on the mayor that morning and the killing "to-day," the Times-Recorder put the killing about midnight Monday, and the Iowa County Democrat's version, dated August 23, said the attack came "Tuesday morning." The condensed briefs placed Mayor Wilson in Cordele, the dispatch's dateline, whereas the fuller reports put both the attack and the killing at Seville.
